questions.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ 7 & 1\end{aligned}].

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-(1)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +5+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-4I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & 5 \\ b & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{a}{b}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & 15 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{5}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ -12 & 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -12 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 0 \\ -12 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. On the other hand, from the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$,

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]

questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 2 \\ -1 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-2\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda +1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{4}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Determine if the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069391/assets/dfc9ee546f72ad68cf116b8f67d165ba9b6ff6e77dce88f145dda93f13091441.png)
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-3I\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.
